readerTitle: Why the same ride costs more at midnight
caseNote: 실제 기업·연구 (Uber 서지 프라이싱 사례 연구, Coca-Cola 1999년 자판기 발언, Wendy's 2024년 발언) + 가상 적용 (승차 앱, 지역 배송 회사)
insight: 동적 가격의 본업은 손님에게서 더 짜내는 것이 아니다. 고정되어 있고 사라지는 용량을 오르내리는 수요에 맞추는 것이다. 바쁜 시간에는 가격으로 배분하고, 한가한 시간에는 가격으로 채운다.
misconception: 동적 가격은 바쁠 때 값을 올려 폭리를 취하는 수단일 뿐이다. 가격을 고정해 두는 것이 늘 더 공정하다.

sources.text: Hall, J., Kendrick, C., & Nosko, C. (2015). The Effects of Uber's Surge Pricing: A Case Study. Uber / University of Chicago.
Coca-Cola CEO M. Douglas Ivester, interview with Veja (Brazil), October 1999, as reported by The New York Times and others
Wendy's Q4 2023 earnings call (February 2024) and the company's follow-up statement on dynamic pricing
Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J., & Thaler, R. (1986). Fairness as a Constraint on Profit Seeking. American Economic Review.

factChecks.note: Uber 사례 연구의 콘서트는 2015년 3월 매디슨 스퀘어 가든의 Ariana Grande 공연입니다. 카드에는 가수 이름을 쓰지 않고 'a sold-out concert at Madison Square Garden'으로 적었습니다. 서지 후 대기 시간이 짧게 유지되고 운전자 공급이 늘었다는 서술이 원문과 맞는지 확인하세요.
2014→2015 새해 전야 뉴욕에서 서지 기능이 오류로 꺼진 시간은 원문 기준 약 26분입니다. 카드에는 'a short stretch'로만 적었습니다. 그동안 대기 시간이 늘고 처리된 요청 비율이 크게 떨어졌다는 서술을 원문 그래프와 대조하세요.
Coca-Cola: 1999년 10월 Ivester가 Veja 인터뷰에서 더운 날 자동으로 가격이 오르는 자판기를 언급했고, 반발이 나오자 회사는 도입 계획이 없다고 밝혔습니다. 직접 인용은 쓰지 않고 요약만 했습니다. Ivester의 같은 해 사임과 인과관계는 주장하지 않습니다.
Wendy's: 2024년 2월 실적 발표에서 CEO Kirk Tanner가 디지털 메뉴판과 함께 'dynamic pricing' 시험을 언급했습니다. 반발 후 회사는 바쁜 시간에 가격을 올리는 '서지 프라이싱'은 하지 않으며 한가한 시간 할인을 염두에 뒀다고 해명했습니다. 게시 전 보도자료 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
승차 앱(2번 카드)과 배송 회사(8번 카드) 상황은 가상 사례이며 수치(밴 20대 등)는 설명용입니다.

cards.title: Why the same ride costs more at midnight
body: New Year's Eve, just after midnight. Thousands of people in one city open a ride app at the same moment. There are far fewer drivers on the road than riders who want to go home.
Someone will wait. The question is who, and for how long. The price is about to decide.

image.label: Crowd on a city street at midnight, phones raised, few cars
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 새해 자정 직후 도심 거리, 휴대폰을 든 사람들이 길게 서 있고 도로에는 차가 두세 대뿐. 하늘에 작은 불꽃. 실제 앱 로고나 브랜드 표시는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Requests just jumped far above your drivers.
body: You run a ride app. On a big holiday night, ride requests suddenly outnumber available drivers many times over.
What do you do with the price?

options.text: Keep the normal price. Raising it tonight would look greedy
options.feedback: The price looks fair, but the cars don't stretch. Whoever taps first gets a ride, and most people get nothing but a long wait.

options.text: Raise the price while demand outruns drivers, and show it before riders book
options.feedback: A higher price pulls more drivers onto the road and lets riders who can wait choose to wait. You trade some goodwill for rides that actually happen.

options.text: Raise it, but cap the increase at 10%
options.feedback: A small cap softens the backlash. It may also be too small to bring out extra drivers or shorten the line.

cards.title: Uber's economists watched it happen.
body: In a 2015 case study, Uber economists looked at a sold-out concert at Madison Square Garden. When the show ended, requests spiked and prices rose. More drivers headed to the area, and wait times stayed short.

They also studied an accident. On New Year's Eve 2014, a glitch switched off surge pricing in New York for **a short stretch**. Waits grew longer, and a far smaller share of requests got a car. The price had been doing real work.

cards.title: Dynamic pricing
body: **Dynamic pricing** means changing the price as demand and supply change, often by the hour or the day.

It differs from price discrimination, which charges different customers different prices. Dynamic pricing changes the price based on *when*, not *who*. Everyone booking at the same moment sees the same price.
Its main job is to match limited capacity to demand that rises and falls.

image.label: Price line rising and falling with a demand curve over a day
image.brief: 하루 24시간 가로축 그래프. 회색 영역은 수요(아침·저녁에 높음), 그 위를 따라 오르내리는 가격 선. 수요가 높을 때 'Ration the peak', 낮을 때 'Fill the quiet hours' 라벨.

cards.title: It fits when capacity can't flex.
body: Dynamic pricing earns its keep under a few conditions:
list: **Capacity is fixed** or slow to add: seats, rooms, drivers, machines
**Capacity perishes:** an empty hotel room tonight can't be sold tomorrow
**Demand swings** by hour, day or season
**Changing prices is cheap:** an app, a screen, a booking system
cards.callout: A higher price rations the peak. A lower price fills the quiet hours.

cards.title: The quiet hours matter just as much.
body: Most people picture dynamic pricing as prices going up. Much of its value comes from prices going down.

Happy hour at a bar, cheaper off-peak train tickets, early-bird dinners and lower hotel rates midweek all use the same idea. They move customers who are flexible into times when capacity would otherwise sit empty.
That spreads demand out, so the business serves more people with the same seats, rooms or staff.

cards.title: Same math, very different reactions.
body: In 1999, Coca-Cola's CEO told a Brazilian magazine that a vending machine could charge more on hot days. The backlash was swift, and the company said it had no plans for such machines. In 2024, Wendy's mentioned testing dynamic pricing and faced a similar outcry. It then said it meant discounts in slow hours, not surge prices.
Research on fairness finds people accept a discount at quiet times far more easily than a surcharge at busy ones. Cap the peak and publish the rules.

image.label: Vending machine with a thermometer and an angry speech bubble
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 무지 자판기 옆에 온도계가 높게 올라가 있고 가격표가 커지는 모습, 옆에 화난 말풍선 하나. 실제 음료 브랜드 로고나 병 모양은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Now it's a delivery company.
body: You run a regional delivery firm with 20 vans. Business customers book same-day pickups.
Friday afternoons are overbooked: you turn away orders and pay overtime. On Tuesday mornings, half the vans sit idle. What do you change?

options.text: Raise all prices by 15% to cover the Friday overtime
options.feedback: You earn more per job, but nothing moves. Friday stays jammed, and Tuesday gets even quieter as price-sensitive customers leave.

options.text: Publish slot prices: a modest premium on Friday afternoons, a clear discount on Tuesday mornings
options.feedback: Flexible customers shift to cheap slots, and the busy slot pays for itself. Publishing prices in advance, and leading with the discount, keeps it feeling fair.

options.text: Buy five more vans to handle Fridays
options.feedback: Friday gets easier, but you now pay for five vans that sit idle most of the week. Try shifting demand before buying capacity.

cards.title: Let the price move when your capacity can't.
body: When capacity is fixed and demand swings, a single price leaves you turning customers away at the peak and idle in the quiet hours. A moving price can fix both, if customers see the rules as fair.
**Try it today:** find your busiest and quietest hour or day. Write down one price change that would move a few customers from the first to the second.
